author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution first **rewires the tree** and then **counts subtree sizes**. For every node `i` (except the root), it walks up the original `parent` chain until it finds an ancestor `p` whose character `s[p]` matches `s[i]`; if such an ancestor exists, `newParent[i]` is set to that ancestor, otherwise the original parent is kept. It then builds an adjacency list `graph` from `newParent`, initializes `dp` with `1` for every node (each node counts itself), and runs a recursive `explore` DFS from the root that adds each child's subtree size into its parent's `dp` entry before returning it. The returned `dp` array holds the subtree size of every node in the modified tree. The drawback is the ancestor search: in a deep chain-like tree with few matching characters, each node may climb almost all the way to the root, making the first phase **O(n²)** in the worst case, which is why it times out.

author: Vitor + ChatGPT
notes: Rewiring while traversing: great for performance, so much more complicated to fully grasp.
aiExplanation: This solution finds the closest matching ancestor for every node **during a single DFS** instead of climbing the tree repeatedly. It builds a child adjacency list `graph` from the original `parent` array and keeps a 26-slot `last` array (one per lowercase letter) that records the **nearest ancestor on the current DFS path** having that character, or `-1` if none. When visiting a node, it reads `prev = last[char]` to learn its new parent `p` (falling back to the original `parent[node]` when there is no matching ancestor), temporarily sets `last[char] = node` so descendants see it, recurses into all children, and then **restores** `last[char] = prev` so siblings are not affected. Because children finish before the parent, by the time the recursion unwinds `res[node]` already holds the full subtree size, so it is added into `res[p]` in a bottom-up manner. Every node is visited once and the ancestor lookup is constant time, giving **O(n)** overall.
